stories.summary: Akakū covered the Saturday parade, and intern Maddie Baldwin's report highlights the floats, Paʻu Riders, honoree Kaonoulu Ranch and grand marshal Brenda Kuwala-Ao.
stories.text: Aloha. I'm Maddie Baldwin, born and raised right here in Makauao and I'm so excited to welcome you to the 58th annual Makauao Parade, legendary in showcasing the best of upcountry and paʻaniolo culture. Besides celebrating the parade, we are also celebrating 110 years of Kaonoulu Ranch and 250 years of America. How amazing that they're all coming together for this year's Fourth of July Celebration Week. This year is as exciting as ever with classic cars showcased by Maui classic cruisers, decorated floats from local organizations and businesses, and the highly anticipated Pā'u riders wearing the colors of their island's And a signature flower. With it being an election year, we're also seeing a lot of the candidates running for the 2026 election. And as always, it's so exciting to see families, community, and visitors all come together. This year's Community Honoree is the historic Kaonōulu Ranch, home to the Oski Rice Event Center, and host of our favorite community events, Including the annual 4th of July Makoau Stampede. We have four generations of cowboys riding for them today. This year's grand marshal is Brenda Kuwala-Ao, selected in recognition of her dedication to the upcountry Maui community. Brenda's diverse background includes barrel racing, community development, and a 37-year career in radio broadcasting. Wow, what an amazing year this is for the parade. If you want to see the full live broadcast with Patty Lee and Joe Abella, check that out on Akakū's YouTube channel. Mahalo for joining me today and we'll see you again next year.

stories.headline: Olowalu coast faces sea level rise; reef at risk
stories.summary: A July 9 presentation will address sea level rise along the Olowalu coast, and a report describes the reef's importance and threats from coastal development.
stories.text: There is no place on Earth quite like the amazing coral reefs at Oluwalu. Biologist Hannah Bernard explains. One of the most amazing places in Hawaiʻi. In fact, on the planet. And that's because right here at Oluwalu, we have a really large aggregate coral structure, which means that the base of this reef is dead coral, coral skeleton According to the Maui Nui Marine Resource Council, the reef is home to the largest known manta ray population in the United States. The Oluwalu Reef also acts as a coral nursery And if we change the shoreline, if we create more impervious surfaces, if we build more close to the coast, and we create more of a possibility of nutrient runoff and sediment runoff, then we change this place. And all of the life that's dependent on it may shift or it may begin to degrade. And that's what we've seen. We've seen this unfortunately The Oluwalu Reef has already stressed. Nearly 50% of the reef suffered bleaching in 2015. Some of its oldest coral is nearly 90% dead. Siding rates for manta rays have dropped by In the past few decades, our track record as ocean stewards is dismal, as many once-thriving reefs are near collapse. Right down the coast of Ma'alai village, only 4% of coral cover remains, reminding us how building next to these complex ecosystems can silt out and choke our reefs. This area is a critical habitat to many rare and endangered animals, from the ancient kūpuna corals to turtles, mantas, and monk seals. Will this project be pushed through, plowing over the warnings from scientists and the concerns of citizens? Is there a way to have affordable housing and protect the most important reef in Maui waters? We'll just have to wait and see.

stories.headline: UH study finds pueo often killed by vehicles
stories.summary: More than half of 243 owl deaths from 1993 to 2025 were trauma mostly caused by cars, and drivers are urged to watch carefully in mornings and evenings.
stories.text: The Pueo, or Hawaiian short-eared owl, according to legend, is a sign of good luck and appears to help people in times of stress. The problem, according to a recent UH study, is that they Other ones likely to be stressed or even killed by careless motorists. Pueo like to hunt near roadways and more than half of the 243 owl deaths from 1993 to 2025 can be attributed to trauma mostly caused by cars. stories.text: A decade after launching in West Maui, Huiʻōkawaeola is expanding its long-term coastal water quality monitoring program to Molokaʻi's south shore. The effort will establish five permanent monitoring The sites between Kalamaula and Kakahaya Park collecting data on sediment, nutrients, bacteria, and other pollutants that can impact coral reefs and human health. Organizers say the expansion responds to requests from Molokaʻi leaders and residents seeking better information to protect nearshore waters.

stories.headline: Organizers and county on Wailuku Film Festival opening night
stories.summary: Festival organizers and a county representative describe opening night at the new Naylor Theatre and why they backed a film festival to help revive Wailuku Town.
stories.text: We're here at the brand new Naylor Theatre. Tell us what's happening tonight. This fits into the broader ecosystem of nurturing local talent, showing them how you can create content for yourself, but there's actually a way to get it out there into the world, potentially monetize it. And I'm most excited about the fact that we have so many filmmakers attending the festival, and I get to introduce them to one another, and they can talk about their films and potentially generate films together. And thanks to Akakū for being a partner in this inaugural year. Our pleasure. Brian was telling us that the county was very, very supportive in all of the endeavors. Tell us, why did you get behind this idea in the first place? Well, a couple of reasons. First of all, being in Wailuku. Coming back to Wailuku, I think, is something that is exciting. And you can just tell by the buzz, folks that are down at E.L. Theatre, folks that are in this theatre here. So, number one, it was just the location. We want to continue to revive Wailuku Town. And then of course just the film industry itself. You know, that's something that we can have a bigger part of in Maui and what's seen as our isolated state. We can add a lot to this creative industry, especially this. And I think we're going to see a lot of talented directors and film producers. And I'm looking forward to seeing the films. stories.headline: Matt Yamashita on documentary about Hui o Waʻa Kaulua

stories.text: We're here with Matt Yamashita, who has a film here in the Wailuku Film Festival. Tell us a little bit about your film. Our film is a 20-minute short documentary. It's called Hui o Waʻa Kaulua. And it's the story of Huiawaʻa Kauluwa, which is a Maui non-profit that has been sailing traditional Hawaiian waʻa since the 1970s. And it's a story that was never told until now, and it's a story that needs to be told because they have been around for many decades, and they've done amazing things for the community, especially after the Lahaina fire. It's a story of resilience and how they came back and how they gave back to the community that they were born out of. And how they continue to grow today and continue to give back. stories.headline: Kīhei Public Library celebrates 30th anniversary
stories.summary: The Kīhei Public Library marked its 30th anniversary with live Hawaiian music, books and young readers.
stories.text: Follow a wee lad who refused to wear a shirt through the doors of Kīhei Public Library and you'll find more than just books. In the bay window, Maui musician Anthony Fluke filled the room with live Hawaiian music as young readers browse shelves of books, comics, and even the library's Lego collection. The celebration marked the library's 30th anniversary, bringing together families, staff, and community members to honor three decades of learning, storytelling, and connection in South Maui. Fluke, a Nāhoku Hanohano Award finalist and Kīhei-born musician known for his original Hawaiian and slack kī music, provided the soundtrack for the afternoon as Keiki explored, read, built, and discovered. Organizers say the milestone celebration was a reminder that the library remains one of Kīhei's most welcoming community gathering place.
